title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
summary: Diagnose in adults with 2 of ovulatory dysfunction, hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound or raised AMH, after excluding mimics; screen all for dysglycaemia (OGTT), lipids, blood pressure and depression; use lifestyle, the COCP and metformin for symptoms and metabolic risk; and use letrozole first line for anovulatory infertility.

sections.title: Diagnose (adults)
items: Two of: (1) ovulatory dysfunction or irregular cycles, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound or a raised AMH, after excluding other causes (2023 International Guideline, built on the Rotterdam criteria).

Irregular cycles from 3 years after menarche: cycles shorter than 21 or longer than 35 days, or fewer than 8 cycles a year; any single cycle over 90 days after the first year. Ovulatory dysfunction can occur with regular cycles (check mid-luteal progesterone).
When irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism are both present, ultrasound and AMH are not needed for diagnosis.
Hirsutism: modified Ferriman-Gallwey score of 4 to 6 or more depending on ethnicity; hirsutism alone predicts biochemical hyperandrogenism. Acne or female-pattern hair loss alone are weak predictors.
Adolescents need both irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism; do not use ultrasound or AMH within 8 years of menarche. If criteria are incomplete, label as increased risk and reassess.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Biochemical hyperandrogenism: total and free testosterone (free androgen index), ideally by LC-MS/MS; if normal, consider androstenedione and DHEAS. If on the COCP, stop it for at least 3 months when androgen testing is essential.

Exclude mimics: pregnancy test, TSH, prolactin, 17-hydroxyprogesterone (non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia), and FSH and oestradiol if hypothalamic amenorrhoea or premature ovarian insufficiency is possible.
Markedly raised androgens, rapid virilisation or new severe hirsutism: exclude an androgen-secreting tumour, Cushing syndrome and, after menopause, ovarian hyperthecosis.

Ultrasound (transvaginal preferred): follicle number per ovary 20 or more in at least one ovary; with older equipment or transabdominal scans use ovarian volume 10 mL or more or 10 or more follicles per section.
AMH can replace ultrasound for polycystic morphology in adults using assay-specific cut-offs; never use AMH as a single diagnostic test and do not do both AMH and ultrasound.

sections.title: Screen for metabolic and other risks
items: 75 g OGTT at diagnosis in all, regardless of BMI (fasting glucose or HbA1c if OGTT is not possible); reassess glycaemic status every 1 to 3 years according to risk.
Lipid profile at diagnosis; blood pressure yearly and when planning pregnancy.
Screen for depression and anxiety at diagnosis, and be alert to eating disorders and body image distress.
Ask about snoring, unrefreshing sleep and daytime sleepiness: obstructive sleep apnoea is more common in PCOS independent of BMI.

Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer risk is increased; routine screening is not advised, but investigate a thickened endometrium (biopsy and withdrawal bleed) especially with long-standing amenorrhoea, higher weight or diabetes.
Weigh with consent and explain weight-related risks; insulin assays are not recommended in routine care.

sections.title: Lifestyle, cycles and hyperandrogenism
items: Healthy eating and physical activity for all (150 to 300 minutes of moderate or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity per week); if weight loss is a goal, prescribe a tailored energy deficit. Preventing weight gain matters at every BMI.

COCP first line for irregular cycles and hirsutism: use the lowest effective dose (20 to 30 mcg ethinylestradiol); no specific preparation is preferred. 35 mcg ethinylestradiol with cyproterone acetate is second line because of VTE risk. Apply standard contraindication criteria.
Not on the COCP with infrequent cycles: protect the endometrium with a progestogen.

Hirsutism: mechanical laser or light therapy for facial hair. If the response to 6 months of COCP or cosmetic therapy is poor, add an anti-androgen such as spironolactone 25 to 100 mg/day, always with effective contraception (risk of male fetal undervirilisation).
Inositol may be used on patient preference but has limited clinical benefit; metformin is more effective for hirsutism and central adiposity.

sections.title: Metabolic treatment
items: Metformin for adults with BMI 25 kg/m2 or more to improve weight, insulin resistance, glucose and lipids (may be considered below 25); it is about as effective as active lifestyle change.
Start metformin at 500 mg daily and increase by 500 mg every 1 to 2 weeks; extended-release tablets improve tolerance; maximum 2.5 g/day. Check vitamin B12 in those at risk on long-term use.
Add metformin to the COCP mainly at high metabolic risk: BMI above 30 kg/m2, impaired glucose tolerance, diabetes risk factors or a high-risk ethnic group such as South Asian women.
Anti-obesity medicines (GLP-1 RA such as semaglutide or liraglutide, or orlistat) can be used as in the general population, with effective contraception; bariatric surgery can also be considered.

sections.title: Anovulatory infertility
items: Before ovulation induction: semen analysis, consider tubal patency testing, and optimise weight, blood pressure, smoking, alcohol and glycaemia (OGTT); start folic acid (higher dose if BMI above 30 kg/m2).

Letrozole is first line for ovulation induction (off-label in many countries): typically 2.5 mg daily for 5 days from day 3 of a spontaneous or progestogen-induced bleed, increased by 2.5 mg per cycle to 7.5 mg if there is no ovulation. Exclude pregnancy first.
Alternatives: clomiphene citrate (ultrasound monitoring for multiple pregnancy), clomiphene plus metformin, or metformin alone (less effective).
Second line: low-dose step-up gonadotrophins (cancel if more than 2 follicles over 14 mm) or laparoscopic ovarian surgery; IVF third line with single embryo transfer.

PCOS pregnancies are high risk: OGTT before conception or at booking, and again at 24 to 28 weeks; monitor blood pressure, weight gain and fetal growth. Metformin is not routinely recommended in pregnancy.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Diagnosing PCOS from an ultrasound or AMH result alone, without ovulatory dysfunction or hyperandrogenism.
Using ultrasound to diagnose PCOS in adolescents.
Missing thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, non-classic CAH or an androgen-secreting tumour.
Starting spironolactone or a GLP-1 RA without reliable contraception.
Relying on fasting glucose alone; an OGTT detects more dysglycaemia in PCOS.

drugs.name: Combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol 20 to 30 mcg)
drugs.dose: 1 tablet orally daily as per pack regimen
drugs.notes: First line for cycles and hirsutism. Check contraindications (migraine with aura, VTE risk, smoking over 35).

drugs.name: Ethinylestradiol 35 mcg with cyproterone acetate 2 mg
drugs.dose: 1 tablet orally daily as per pack regimen
drugs.notes: Second line because of higher VTE risk.

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.dose: 500 mg orally daily, increased by 500 mg every 1 to 2 weeks; maximum 2.5 g/day
drugs.notes: Extended release improves GI tolerance. Monitor vitamin B12 if at risk.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.notes: Hirsutism after 6 months of COCP; effective contraception essential.

drugs.name: Letrozole
drugs.dose: 2.5 mg orally daily for 5 days (days 3 to 7), increasing by 2.5 mg per cycle to a maximum of 7.5 mg
drugs.notes: First line for ovulation induction; off-label in many countries. Exclude pregnancy first.

drugs.name: Clomiphene citrate
drugs.dose: 50 mg orally daily for 5 days from day 2 to 5 of the cycle, increased by 50 mg per cycle to a maximum of 150 mg
